overview: This file traces Japanese gold policy and production from 1934 to 1939, beginning with a reference to regulations implementing Japan’s gold-purchasing law, continuing with a detailed 1938 U.S. Military Attaché report on plans to expand gold output throughout Japan and its colonial and occupied territories, and ending with references to reports on Japan’s gold position, exports, and bank reserves in late 1939. The principal report translates an article by mining executive Ichiro Koyama and supplies production estimates for mines in Japan, Korea, Manchukuo, China, and Taiwan, while describing subsidies, import and railway concessions, government control, and a five-year expansion program intended to support wartime imports and stabilize the yen.

people.role: Japanese Foreign Minister and former Governor-General of Korea

subfiles.title: Reference to report on Japan’s gold-purchasing regulations
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to Commercial Attaché report no. 114 concerning regulations under Japan’s gold-purchasing law.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to file 102.81 Tokyo/342 for report no. 114, dated April 13, 1934. That report concerned Japanese gold-purchasing regulations announced in the Official Gazette on April 7, 1934.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 9481: Plan for Increase in Gold Production
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report translates and comments upon Ichiro Koyama’s survey of Japanese plans to expand gold production across the empire and neighboring occupied areas.
subfiles.summary: Koyama links the drive for gold to the immense cost of Japan’s war in China, its trade deficit, military imports, and continental industrial expansion. He reviews subsidies, state purchasing and control, import-duty exemptions, reduced railway charges, production figures, and mining prospects in Korea, Manchukuo, China, Taiwan, and Japan proper. The government’s five-year plan sought to raise annual imperial output from roughly ¥200 million to ¥500 million through expanded production and a semipublic Gold Mining Promotion Company. Koyama criticizes companies for leaving claims idle and recommends compulsory development, joint management of adjacent properties, and central processing plants; Creswell concludes that substantial gains are plausible but unlikely to appear immediately.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Japan’s gold situation
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a Kobe report on Japan’s gold situation filed elsewhere in the decimal records.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference identifies a report from Gourley at Kobe dated September 30, 1939. The original document is filed under number 894.515/64 rather than with this gold-mining file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on accelerated gold exports and reduced bank reserves
subfiles.about: The sheet references a report on Japan’s acceleration of gold exports and reduction of bank gold reserves in late 1939.
subfiles.summary: The referenced Kobe report described Japan as speeding up gold exports while reducing bank gold reserves during the latter part of 1939. Dated December 22, 1939, the original is filed as 894.515/66.

interest: The file is especially valuable for its unusually detailed contemporary inventory of producing mines, refineries, output values, and expansion prospects throughout Japan’s imperial economic sphere. It shows how gold policy was tied directly to the financing of the war in China, the import of munitions, exchange-rate stability, and colonial resource extraction. Koyama’s criticism of dormant mining claims also reveals disagreement within Japanese industry over how far the state should compel production, while the 1939 cross-references connect mining policy to the subsequent depletion and export of monetary gold.
